title: Women’s football is booming. Nearly half of surveyed players are considering leaving early
subtitle: A survey of 791 players across 40 countries finds that the women’s game is creating global stars faster than it is creating secure jobs. The warning is not that women lack ambition, but that professional expectations are still being imposed without professional protection.
author: ATHENA
body:
Nearly half of the women footballers surveyed for a new global employment report said they were considering leaving the game earlier than planned, even as salaries, audiences and commercial investment rise at the top of the sport.

The study by global players’ union FIFPRO gathered survey responses from 791 players in 40 countries during the 2025–26 season and conducted semi-structured interviews with 34 players across six regions. Forty-nine per cent of respondents said they were considering an early departure. Among that group, 59% cited their financial situation and 46% cited psychological stress; respondents could identify more than one reason, so those percentages should not be added together. [1], [2].

The result does not mean that half of all professional women footballers will retire soon. It records what this group was considering when surveyed, not completed retirements or a forecast. The sample is broad but not a random census of every league and player in the world, and FIFPRO is a union advocating for stronger labour standards. Its figures should be read as substantial evidence of insecurity among surveyed players, not a precise estimate for every woman who plays professionally.

The report nevertheless exposes a contradiction the industry cannot explain away. Women’s football increasingly presents itself as a major commercial product. Many of the women producing that product still cannot depend on it as stable employment.

## A rising average can conceal the player in the middle

FIFPRO reports that the inflation-adjusted average monthly club wage in its survey has tripled since its previous global study in 2017, reaching $2,601. The median is considerably lower at $1,669.

That difference matters. An average can be pulled upwards by a relatively small number of highly paid players in wealthy leagues. The median—the point at which half of reported salaries fall above and half below—better describes the centre of an unequal distribution. Neither figure is a universal wage: taxes, living costs, season length and whether players are paid throughout the year differ by country.

In ten Eastern European countries analysed, average pay remained below the relevant national minimum wage, FIFPRO said. Even in parts of Western Europe and Asia-Oceania containing prominent leagues, average player pay was not substantially higher than national minimums. These are regional comparisons within the report; they do not mean every club or player in those regions has the same conditions.

Employment security is also about more than the amount deposited each month. Only 56% of respondents had an employment contract, according to FIFPRO, while the average contract lasted 19 months. Just 13% received a pension from their club, and only eight of the 30 national leagues examined had a collective agreement negotiated with players through their unions.

A short contract can turn an injury, pregnancy, coaching change or missed renewal into an immediate housing and income problem. It also makes long-term financial planning unusually difficult for workers whose careers are already brief.

Calling a league professional does not by itself make every player’s job professional. That status should be visible in written employment rights, reliable pay, medical care, qualified staff and a procedure through which a player can challenge a club without sacrificing her career.

## Mental health cannot be separated from working conditions

Fifty-seven per cent of surveyed players reported having struggled with their mental health. Half of those players said their clubs had not provided support.

The survey does not diagnose a clinical condition, establish when each difficulty began or prove that football caused it. Financial insecurity, injury, personal circumstances and pressures outside the sport can overlap. FIFPRO’s player interviews did, however, identify workload and social-media abuse among the pressures accompanying the game’s expansion. [3].

Mental-health provision should therefore not be reduced to teaching players to tolerate an unstable workplace. Confidential care needs to be independent enough for a player to seek help without fearing that disclosures will affect team selection, contract renewal or how coaches assess her resilience.

FIFPRO points to the United States’ National Women’s Soccer League, where mental-health practitioners work alongside club staff and players have access to extended mental-health leave, as one possible model. A policy on paper still needs qualified clinicians, privacy protections and enough staffing to work in practice.

The staffing problem extends beyond counselling. Forty-seven per cent of respondents said their clubs lacked sufficient staff for players’ needs. FIFPRO’s interviews included accounts of inexperienced or underqualified support personnel. As teams demand more training, travel, media work and matches from players, medical, safeguarding and performance services have to grow with those obligations.

## Maternity protections show that rules can change expectations

The report also contains evidence of progress. Among players considering an early exit, the proportion citing starting a family fell from 47% in FIFPRO’s 2017 study to 19% in 2026.

FIFPRO connects that shift partly to global maternity protections introduced by FIFA in 2021 and expanded in 2024, as well as to the visibility of players combining parenthood with elite sport. FIFA’s rules include paid maternity leave and protections relating to adoption, non-biological motherhood, severe menstrual symptoms, pregnancy complications and returning to football. [4].

The comparison is encouraging, but it is not a controlled experiment. The 2017 and 2026 samples are not identical, the industry changed in other ways and a reduced intention to leave is not proof that every club implements the rules properly.

Individual cases demonstrate why enforcement matters. In a ruling publicised in June, the Court of Arbitration for Sport found that Lazio Women unlawfully ended Swedish defender Maja Gothberg’s employment after learning she was pregnant and awarded compensation. Lazio said the dispute arose from misunderstandings during a complex negotiation and promised to review its procedures. The decision showed that maternity rules can create a remedy, not merely a public commitment. [5], [6].

FIFPRO argues that another gap remains: pregnancy does not automatically extend a contract. With an average contract length of only 19 months, leave protections can be weakened if a player’s agreement simply expires during pregnancy or recovery.

New fertility benefits create a related question. Chelsea and Spain’s football federation have offered players access to services including egg freezing. Such programmes may expand reproductive choice, but employer-funded treatment must not become pressure to postpone motherhood for a club’s convenience. Access to fertility care and the right to become pregnant during a playing career should exist together. [7].

## Growth should be measured by the careers it sustains

The solution is not to ask supporters to feel guilty about sold-out stadiums or higher broadcast revenues. Commercial growth can finance better employment. The accountability question is where that money travels after it enters the sport.

League licensing can require minimum staffing, safe facilities, medical cover and written contracts. Collective bargaining can give players a role in determining salaries, leave, scheduling and dispute procedures. Governing bodies can make funding conditional on verified labour standards rather than accepting the word “professional” as proof of professional conditions.

Clubs should also publish enough information to make progress measurable: how many players are employees, whether wages arrive on time, which healthcare services are independent, how maternity rules are implemented and whether athletes have a protected route to report abuse or unsafe conditions.

Women players have already demonstrated the demand for their sport. They have also organised through unions, challenged discriminatory decisions and helped establish maternity rights that were once absent from the global rulebook.

The new report is not evidence that women are walking away because they cannot withstand elite competition. It is evidence that talent and commitment cannot indefinitely substitute for employment security.

A sport has not fully professionalised when its stars play in packed stadiums while the player beside them is one short contract, one injury or one unpaid month away from leaving. Women’s football should judge its growth not only by the audiences it attracts, but by how many women can build—and finish—the careers their ability earned.
